name: BMW M5 (E39)
engine: 4.9L S62 V8 (badged 5.0), double-VANOS with individual throttle bodies
transmission: 6-speed manual only (Getrag 420G) in the US — no automatic offered
reliability: 8/10 — the E39 M5 is often called the definitive analog super-sedan: a hand-built 4.9L V8, a 6-speed manual, an understated four-door body, and no electronic gimmickry. Mechanically the S62 is strong, with well-mapped age items rather than nasty surprises — VANOS wear (especially early 1999 units), timing-chain guide rattle at high mileage, and a healthy appetite for oil that is normal by design. Keep the cooling system fresh and the VANOS serviced and it's one of the most satisfying, usable fast cars ever made. Values reflect that reputation.
cost_to_own: Insurance: Moderate–High (appreciating modern classic) · Maintenance ~$1,500/yr; the S62 is not cheap to service · Clean, unmodified manual cars are firmly appreciating
popular_mods: A VANOS rebuild/refresh to restore crisp response and quiet the growl
A full cooling-system overhaul (water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, radiator)
A quality shock/spring or coilover refresh with fresh bushings
A sensible exhaust to let the S62 V8 breathe and sing
Honest take: it's near-perfect stock — the best money goes into VANOS, cooling, and originality, not power
oil_type: 10W-60 full synthetic (BMW M-spec; LL-98 5W-30 was later approved, but 10W-60 is preferred)

generations.E39 M5 (2000–2003 US): The analog benchmark — 394 hp 4.9L S62 V8, 6-speed manual only, roughly 20,000 built worldwide. Often cited as 'peak BMW M' for pairing near-supercar pace with everyday civility and zero gimmickry.
generations.S62 engine note: The S62 shares its double-VANOS, individual-throttle-body architecture with BMW's other great M engines of the era; it is robust but wants disciplined maintenance.

common_issues: VANOS wear — failed solenoids/seals causing rough idle, a growling noise, and lost power (early 1999 units especially)
Timing-chain guide and tensioner wear producing rattle at higher mileage
High oil consumption by design (loose tolerances; ~1 qt / 1,500 mi is considered normal)
Rod-bearing wear — a shared S62 concern, less severe than the later S85 but present
Cooling-system components (water pump, expansion tank, thermostat) age out and fail
maintenance_tips: Service the VANOS proactively — it's the defining S62 maintenance item
Refresh the whole cooling system on any car with unknown history
Use the correct 10W-60 M-spec synthetic and check the oil often, given the normal consumption
Inspect timing-chain guides at high mileage and listen for cold-start rattle
Buy on condition and history — a well-kept, documented manual car is worth the premium

engine.detail: Hand-built 4.9L S62 V8 (badged 5.0) with double-VANOS and individual throttle bodies - 394 hp, 369 lb-ft, plus a healthy appetite for oil that's normal by design.
engine.watch: VANOS solenoids/seals wear around 60-120k, causing a growl, rough idle and lost power; rod bearings suffer on neglected oil, so run 10W-60 and service the VANOS proactively.

drivetrain.detail: RWD through a Getrag 420G 6-speed manual - the only gearbox offered in the US, no automatic ever built.
drivetrain.watch: The rubber driveshaft flex disc (guibo) cracks with age, giving clunks on gear changes and driveline vibration - inspect it and the clutch on any high-miler.

suspension.detail: Conventional coil-sprung sport suspension - no adaptive dampers, just well-sorted analog geometry on the E39 chassis.
suspension.watch: Front thrust-arm and control-arm bushings wear out, causing a steering shimmy under light braking and a front-end clunk - a classic E39 refresh item.

brakes.detail: Large-for-the-era discs with two-piece floating front rotors riveted to alloy hats to cut unsprung weight.
brakes.watch: Those floating rotors develop rivet play and warp or rattle over time, and replacements aren't cheap - budget for a full set once worn.

electrical.detail: Straightforward for a flagship - DSC stability control and an on-board computer, no fragile electronic gimmickry.
electrical.watch: The instrument-cluster and OBC LCDs suffer dead-pixel rot from aging ribbon cables, making gauges and messages hard to read - common but fixable.
